newsitem.title: USA: New Fed rules make leasing clearer but not better.
newsitem.headline: New Fed rules make leasing clearer but not better.

text.p: WASHINGTON - The Federal Reserve has issued new rules designed to make car leases easier to understand, but you don't have to go into the fine print to understand this basic fact of auto leasing: It's rarely a sound financial move.

To oversimplify, auto leasing usually makes sense in only two situations. It works for business owners who can sometimes take bigger deductions if they lease the company car than buy it. And it works for people who are hell bent on driving newer and more expensive cars than they can actually afford to buy.
Why? When you lease a car for two or three years, you spend less on a monthly basis than you would buying a car, but at the end of the lease, you own no car.

Business people can use that arrangement to deduct their lease costs from their taxable income and save cash to use for other business expenses. Conspicuous consumers like leases because they can make costly new cars more affordable on a monthly basis.

For the rest of the world, there are two cheaper way to get wheels. You can buy an affordable car and keep it for at least one year after it is paid off. Or you can look for a good used car among the thousands of formerly leased vehicles now glutting the market.
Despite those alternatives, leasing has taken off in America. About one of every three new cars driving off the lots are leased, says the Fed.
So the new rules, which don't go into effect for a full year, will be helpful to many. Many companies say they will try to abide by the tougher disclosure requirements before they have to.

Before the rules go into effect, car leasers can protect themselves by bringing their business to dealers who agree to abide by the tougher disclosure rules ahead of schedule. And they can learn a little about their leases, so they understand exactly what they are paying.
The new rules will force dealers to use a new disclosure form, which will soon be available to consumers from the Federal Reserve.
Even without the form, these are the questions you need answered before you can decide if a lease is worthwhile:

-- What is the gross capitalised cost? This is the actual price of the car that's built into the lease. Leasing experts suggest that you first cut your best deal on a car without telling the sales person whether you want to lease or buy. Then negotiate the lease separately.

-- What is the residual value, and how fair is it? That's the amount that the car is going to be worth on the day you return it. To make sure that your dealer is not artificially lowering the residual value, double check it against the Kelley Blue Book Residual Value Guide, available at your local library, bank, dealer, or direct if you dial (800)258-3266.

-- What's the hidden interest cost? In dealer parlance, this is the "lease rate." Even after the Fed rules go into effect, this will not have to be disclosed in percentages, but only in dollar amounts.

Here's how you find it: Subtract the residual value from the capitalised costs, and that will get you the depreciation built into the lease. Then subtract the depreciation from the total payments you will be asked to make on the lease. The dollar amount left is the total interest you'll pay. That dollar amount will be printed plainly on the Fed's disclosure form; you'll be able to shop one lease against another by comparing that figure.

-- To figure out your interest rate, add the car price and the residual value. Divide by 2, and then multiply by the number of years in the lease. Then divide the total interest in dollars you are paying by that figure. That's a complicated formula, but one you can take from lease to lease or dealer to dealer to see if you're getting a good deal.

-- If you'd rather some one else do the number crunching for you, and you are seriously interested in leasing, consider investing $129.95 in a software programme called Expert Lease Pro. This is a lease-vs.-buy calculator that is stuffed with current car data, including retail pricing for all new vehicles, the latest incentives, and lease guide residual value. It can compare leases to see which one is best, or make a lease-vs.-buy calculation for the car you've already picked out. It's available from Chart Software at (800)418-8450.
